attributes.nuance_translation: An expression used to show that (A) belongs to (B), or exists within (B).

attributes.body:
In this expression, がある has the role of describing the noun that follows it. The description that it is giving is '(A) がある (B)' = '(B) has/with (A)'. This type of phrase is called a relative clause (something that describes a noun), and behaves similarly to an adjective.

In English, a relative clause would require a pronoun such as 'who' 誰（だれ）, 'which' どれ, 'that' それ・あれ, 'where' どこ. However, these types of words are not required in Japanese, and the noun will follow がある directly.

Caution

In a relative clause, because (A) is describing (B), (B) will be considered the 'main topic/subject'. This means that は will generally not be used in place of が. However, の can be used instead of が, as showing a relationship between (A) and (B) is one of the main functions of の.

attributes.source: [DBJG] A Dictionary of Basic Japanese Grammar

attributes.description: Treating verbs and state-of-being like adjectives

attributes.body: がある + Noun expresses possession, using a phrase with a noun, the particle が, and the verb ある to describe another noun (e.g., ピアノがあるレストラン = 'a restaurant with a piano'). In these cases, が can be replaced with の without changing the meaning (e.g., ピアノのあるレストラン).

first_relatable.title: がある + Noun
first_relatable.meaning: Noun (B) that has Noun (A), Noun (B) with Noun (A)

attributes.body: がある expresses the existence or possession of inanimate objects, similar to 'there is' or 'I have' in English (e.g., ピアノがある = 'There is a piano' or 'I have a piano'). When combined with a noun, it describes the noun, much like an adjective (e.g., ピアノがあるレストラン = 'A restaurant with a piano'). Remember, ある changes to いる when referring to animate objects.

second_relatable.title: がある + Noun
second_relatable.meaning: Noun (B) that has Noun (A), Noun (B) with Noun (A)
